Front: Three key questions when evaluating dizziness?
Back: Is it dangerous (arrhythmia, TIA/stroke)? Is it vestibular? If vestibular, peripheral or central?
Acute asymmetry of vestibular inputs from the two labyrinths or their central pathways

Front: Symptoms of symmetric bilateral vestibular loss?
Back: Imbalance and oscillopsia, but no vertigo
BPPV or orthostatic hypotension
Posterior circulation TIA (also migraine)
Vestibular migraine or Meniere disease
Unidirectional horizontal, fast phase away from the lesioned ear, suppressed by visual fixation

Front: Nystagmus patterns that indicate a central lesion?
Back: Direction-changing with gaze, downbeat, pure vertical or pure torsional, not suppressed by fixation

Front: Acute prolonged vertigo with a normal head impulse test suggests?
Back: A central cause (e.g., cerebellar or brainstem stroke)
Catch-up saccade after rapid head rotation toward the weak side (deficient VOR)
Diplopia, dysarthria, limb ataxia, numbness, weakness

Front: Dix-Hallpike finding in posterior canal BPPV?
Back: Transient upbeat-torsional nystagmus, upper poles beating toward the lower (affected) ear
<1 min (typically 15-20 s); change in head position: lying down, rising, looking up, rolling over in bed
Otoconia dislodged from the utricle into a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal
Epley repositioning maneuver
No proven benefit unless herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt)

Front: Vestibular suppressants in vestibular neuritis: how long?
Back: First several days only; later they impede central compensation

Front: Acute vestibular syndrome in an older patient with vascular risk factors and no focal signs?
Back: Still evaluate for stroke
Vertigo attacks, ear fullness/pressure/tinnitus, low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss
Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph)
Diuretics and sodium restriction; then intratympanic glucocorticoids or gentamicin
Vertigo minutes to hours, often without headache; motion and visual-motion sensitivity, photophobia
Migraine prophylactic medications; antiemetics for attacks

Front: Why does vestibular schwannoma rarely cause vertigo?
Back: Slow vestibular loss is compensated centrally

Front: Unexplained unilateral sensorineural hearing loss: imaging?
Back: MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium

Front: Most common iatrogenic cause of bilateral vestibular hypofunction?
Back: Aminoglycosides, especially gentamicin
Reduced dynamic visual acuity, abnormal head impulse both directions, Romberg sign, reduced calorics
Vestibular rehabilitation; avoid suppressants
Drop of more than one line with 1-2 Hz head rotation
Fluctuating dizziness >=3 months, worse standing and in complex visual environments; normal or compensated vestibular testing
SSRIs, cognitive-behavioral therapy, vestibular rehabilitation
Brain MRI and full neurologic evaluation
